title.text: SVD and PCA: rotate, stretch, rotate, and keep only what matters

objects.text: How can a huge matrix be squeezed into a few numbers, and how does LoRA fine-tune a large model cheaply?

Mathematics for AI and Machine Learning  |  Session 6 of 18  |  Linear algebra
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to Session 6, the last session of linear algebra. Last time we found directions that a matrix only stretches. Today every matrix gets the same treatment, even a non-square one. We split it into rotate, stretch, rotate, keep the big stretches, and use the idea to compress an image and to reduce data.

We end with how a published method called LoRA uses the same idea to fine-tune large models cheaply.

title.text: Today in one view: what you will leave with

objects.text: By the end of today you can
Describe the singular value decomposition (SVD) as rotate, stretch, rotate, and read its singular values
Build a low-rank approximation of an 8 by 8 image, and choose how many components to keep
Do principal component analysis (PCA) by hand: centre, covariance, top direction, projection and explained variance

slides.notes:
By the end of today you can describe the singular value decomposition, or SVD, as rotate, stretch, rotate, and read its singular values. You can build a low-rank approximation of a small image and choose how many components to keep. And you can do principal component analysis by hand: centre the data, build the covariance matrix, find the top direction, project and measure the explained variance.

We also meet LoRA, the way large models are fine-tuned cheaply. Which of these sounds most useful for your own work?

title.text:
Your two hours: break a matrix
apart, then keep the best terms

objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Pictures first. Then the lab in Python or in a spreadsheet. Then where it shows up in AI.

slides.notes:
We have two hours. Ten minutes to bring back Session 5 and set the question of the day. Thirty-five minutes of ideas, each as a picture and then a small calculation by hand. A ten minute break. Then forty-five minutes of lab, in Python or a spreadsheet, on the same numbers.

We end with where this appears in AI tools, an exit check, and five minutes to save.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  The covariance matrix of two marks has eigenvalues 102 and 2. What do these two numbers mean?
2.  In power iteration, why divide by the largest entry, and what does that entry estimate?
3.  How are the trace and the determinant of a 2 by 2 matrix linked to its eigenvalues?

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 5. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. The covariance matrix of two marks has eigenvalues 102 and 2. What do these two numbers mean? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. Each eigenvalue is the variance of the data along its eigenvector. Almost all the spread lies along the first direction.

Question two. In power iteration, why divide by the largest entry, and what does that entry estimate? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. Dividing keeps the numbers from growing. The largest entry estimates the top eigenvalue.

Question three. How are the trace and the determinant of a 2 by 2 matrix linked to its eigenvalues? Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. The eigenvalues add up to the trace and multiply to the determinant.

If an answer was missing, do not worry. Your notes from last class have it. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Session 5

rows.text: The covariance matrix of two marks has eigenvalues 102 and 2. What do these two numbers mean?
Each eigenvalue is the variance of the data along its eigenvector. Almost all the spread lies along the first direction.
In power iteration, why divide by the largest entry, and what does that entry estimate?
Dividing keeps the numbers from growing. The largest entry estimates the top eigenvalue.
How are the trace and the determinant of a 2 by 2 matrix linked to its eigenvalues?
The eigenvalues add up to the trace and multiply to the determinant.

objects.text: If one surprised you, look back at Session 5 before the lab. Eigenvalues return today.

slides.notes:
The eigenvalues of the covariance matrix, one hundred two and two, are the variances of the data along the two eigenvector directions. Almost all the spread lies along the first one. In power iteration we divide by the largest entry to keep the numbers from growing, and that entry estimates the top eigenvalue.

And the eigenvalues of a two by two matrix add up to its trace and multiply to its determinant. If one of these surprised you, look at Session 5 again before the lab.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: Any matrix written as rotate, stretch, rotate: A = UΣVᵀ.
A stretch factor in Σ. The singular values are listed from largest to smallest.
A matrix rebuilt from only its first few singular values. It needs far fewer numbers to store.
Finding the directions of greatest spread in data, then keeping only the first few.
Fine-tuning: training an already trained model a little more on new data (training is taught in Sessions 7 to 10). LoRA (low-rank adaptation) does it with two thin matrices.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Singular value decomposition (SVD). Any matrix written as rotate, stretch, rotate: A = UΣVᵀ.

Singular value. A stretch factor in Σ. The singular values are listed from largest to smallest.

Low-rank approximation. A matrix rebuilt from only its first few singular values. It needs far fewer numbers to store.

Principal component analysis (PCA). Finding the directions of greatest spread in data, then keeping only the first few.

Fine-tuning and LoRA. Fine-tuning: training an already trained model a little more on new data (training is taught in Sessions 7 to 10). LoRA (low-rank adaptation) does it with two thin matrices.

title.text: Any matrix acts as rotate, stretch, rotate

objects.alt: Any matrix acts as rotate, stretch, rotate

objects.text: A has rows (2, 2) and (−1, 2): rotate, stretch by 3 and 2, rotate (maybe with a mirror flip).

slides.notes:
Take any matrix, here the one with rows two, two and minus one, two. It turns the unit circle into an ellipse, and it always does so in three simple moves. First rotate, so that two special directions, the red arrow v one and the black arrow v two, lie along the axes.

These two directions are called the right singular vectors. The first two panels are zoomed in so you can see them. Second, stretch along the axes, here by three across and by two up. Third, rotate again into the final position. The stretch factors three and two are the singular values.

For some matrices one of the rotations must include a mirror flip, and that is allowed.

title.text:
The singular value
decomposition writes A as UΣVᵀ

objects.alt: The singular value decomposition writes A as UΣVᵀ

rows.text: First rotation. Its rows are the right singular vectors.
The stretch. diag(3, 2): 3 and 2 on the diagonal, zeros elsewhere. Not the sum symbol.
Last rotation. Its columns are the left singular vectors.
U and V are rotations, sometimes with a mirror flip. Tools may flip a pair.

objects.text: A can be any shape, m by n: U is m by m, Σ m by n, V n by n. Singular values are never negative.

slides.notes:
The decomposition fits on one line: A equals U, times Sigma, times V transpose. Read it from the right, because that is the order the moves happen. V transpose rotates first, and its rows are the right singular vectors. Sigma stretches, with the singular values on its diagonal, largest first.

This capital Sigma is a matrix of stretch factors, unrelated to the sum symbol from Session 1. U rotates last, and its columns are the left singular vectors. A tool may print a pair of singular vectors with both signs flipped, which turns a rotation into a mirror image, and both answers are correct.

Unlike eigenvalues, the SVD works for a matrix of any shape, and its singular values are never negative.

title.text: Worked by hand: singular values from AᵀA

objects.text: A has rows (2, 2) and (−1, 2). The singular values are the square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA.
Form AᵀA
Rows (5, 2) and (2, 8). It is symmetric, so Session 5 applies.
Eigenvalues
T = 13 and D = 36. The root of 13² − 4 × 36 is 5. So λ = 9 and 4.
Singular values
σ₁ = the square root of 9 = 3 and σ₂ = the square root of 4 = 2.
Vectors
For λ = 9, v₁ = (1, 2) / the square root of 5 = (0.447, 0.894). Then u₁ = Av₁ / 3 = (0.894, 0.447).

slides.notes:
Session 5 gives us the singular values by hand. Form A transpose times A. For our matrix it has rows five, two and two, eight. That matrix is symmetric, so we can find its eigenvalues from the trace and the determinant. The trace is thirteen and the determinant is thirty-six.

The square root part is the square root of one sixty-nine minus one forty-four, which is five. So the eigenvalues are nine and four. The singular values are their square roots, three and two. For the vectors, the eigenvector of A transpose A for nine is one, two over root five, and we call it v one.

Then u one is A times v one divided by three. For a covariance matrix the eigenvalues and the singular values agree, which is why PCA can use either.

title.text:
A grey-scale image is a matrix of
numbers, and noise spoils its pattern

objects.alt: A grey-scale image is a matrix of numbers, and noise spoils its pattern

objects.text: Illustrative: each cell is 0 (white) to 9 (black). Error = √(sum of the 64 squared cell differences).

slides.notes:
An image is a grid of numbers, so it is a matrix. Our toy image is eight by eight, with each cell between zero for white and nine for black, and you can read every number in the picture. On the left is a clean pattern, the letter H, made of cells with values one and eight.

On the right is the same image after we added random noise of up to two in each cell. We call the noisy image N, to keep the letter A for the small matrix. The numbers are made up to show the arithmetic. The error under the noisy picture is the square root of the sum of the squared differences of all sixty-four cells from the clean one: 8.19.

title.text:
A column times a row makes a rank
1 pattern from only 16 numbers

objects.alt: A column times a row makes a rank 1 pattern from only 16 numbers

objects.text: A column u of 8 numbers times a row vᵀ of 8 numbers. Cell (i, j) is the i-th number of u times the j-th number of v.

runs.text: Every row of the result is a multiple of the row vᵀ. That is rank 1.
Dark cells appear where both numbers are large.

slides.notes:
The building block of a low-rank approximation is a column times a row. Take a column of eight numbers, u, and a row of eight numbers, v transpose. Multiply every pair, so that the cell in row i and column j is the i-th number of u times the j-th number of v.

The result is a grid of sixty-four cells made from only sixteen numbers. Every row of the grid is a multiple of the same row, which is what rank one means. Here u and v are the first singular vectors of our noisy image, so the dark pattern is the best single pattern of this shape. The darkest cells sit where both u and v are large.

title.text:
SVD adds up rank 1 terms, and a low-rank
approximation keeps the first few

objects.alt: SVD adds up rank 1 terms, and a low-rank approximation keeps the first few

rows.text: The i-th singular value of N. Big ones carry the pattern.
The i-th left and right singular vectors, columns of U and V.
How many terms we keep. Rank k means k independent patterns.
A rank k approximation needs k × (m + n + 1) numbers: u, v and σ for each term.

objects.text: The first k terms give the closest rank k matrix to N (the Eckart-Young theorem).

slides.notes:
A low-rank approximation is built from the SVD written as a sum of rank one terms, each one a singular value times a column times a row. The big singular values come first. To approximate the image, keep only the first k terms and drop the rest. Each kept term costs m plus n plus one numbers: the column, the row and the singular value.

For an eight by eight image with k equal to two that is thirty-four numbers instead of sixty-four. A known result, the Eckart-Young theorem, says no other rank k matrix is closer to the matrix you have.

title.text:
Rank 2 removes most of the noise,
and more terms bring the noise back

objects.alt: Rank 2 removes most of the noise, and more terms bring the noise back

objects.text: Error is measured against the clean H. Rank 2 lands closest; rank 3 starts to copy the noise.

slides.notes:
The rebuilt images are scored against the clean pattern, so we are checking how well the approximation recovers the truth. The noisy image has error 8.19. With one term, the error is 15.40, worse, because one pattern cannot draw an H. With two terms the error drops to 4.54 and the H is clear.

With three terms the error rises to 6.73. Rank three is still the closest rank three matrix to the noisy image, but the extra term starts to copy the noise. The clean H has two independent patterns, which is why two is right. In real work you do not know the clean image, so you need a rule.

title.text:
Singular values show how many terms
matter: a few big bars, then a flat tail

objects.alt: Singular values show how many terms matter: a few big bars, then a flat tail

objects.text: The 8 singular values of the noisy image, largest first. The cumulative share is the running total of σ² divided by the total.

runs.text: Two terms hold 97 percent of the total.
The pattern lives in the big values. Random noise spreads thinly over all eight.

slides.notes:
The singular values of the noisy image are in this bar chart, a plot often called a scree plot. There are two big bars, 36.8 and 15.1, and then a flat tail of small ones. The row of percentages is the cumulative share: the running total of the squared singular values divided by their grand total.

Two terms already hold 97 percent. The picture shows why truncation removes noise. The real pattern is concentrated in a few big singular values. Random noise has no preferred direction, so it spreads thinly over all of them.

title.text:
How many terms to keep: three
rules, and what each one needs

rows.text: Add the shares until you reach a target such as 95 percent. Image: k = 2.
The target is a choice. Ask what the next step needs.
Cut where the bars stop falling steeply. Image: after bar 2.
Some plots have no clear elbow.
Try k = 1, 2, 3 and score the model on held-out data: rows kept aside, never used for fitting.
Needs the full pipeline, but is the most honest.

objects.text: Errors from the clean H, for k = 1, 2, 3: 15.40, 4.54, 6.73. We can measure them only because we built the clean image.

slides.notes:
Three rules decide how many terms to keep, and the same rules apply to PCA later today. First, the cumulative share: add up the shares until you reach a target, such as ninety-five percent. For our image that gives two. The target is your choice, so ask what the next step needs.

Second, the elbow: cut where the bars stop falling steeply. Here that is after bar two. Some plots have no clear elbow. Third, test the real task: try one, two and three terms and score the model on held-out data, which means rows you kept aside and never used for fitting. That is the most honest answer.

title.text:
A low-rank approximation stores thin
matrices instead of the whole matrix

objects.alt: A low-rank approximation stores thin matrices instead of the whole matrix

objects.text: Here 34 numbers replace 64. At 1,000 by 1,000 and rank 20: 40,020 against 1,000,000 (illustrative).

slides.notes:
The saving can be drawn. The big matrix is approximately a thin tall matrix U k, times a small square Sigma k, times a thin wide matrix V k transpose. Only the diagonal numbers of Sigma k are stored, the two gold cells. For our image that is thirty-four numbers instead of sixty-four, a modest saving.

The saving grows with size. For a matrix with a thousand rows and a thousand columns, a rank twenty approximation stores about forty thousand numbers instead of one million. That size is illustrative. This is the heart of compression, and, as we will see at the end, of how large models are fine-tuned cheaply.

title.text:
PCA is five steps: centre, covariance,
directions, project, measure

objects.alt: PCA is five steps: centre, covariance, directions, project, measure

objects.text: Principal component analysis (PCA). The directions are the principal components. Steps 1 to 3 are Session 5.

slides.notes:
Principal component analysis, or PCA, is a recipe of five steps, and you already know most of them from Session 5. Centre each column by subtracting its mean. Build the covariance matrix, dividing by n minus one. Find its eigenvectors, largest eigenvalue first. These directions are called the principal components.

Then project: give every row a score, which is how far it sits along a direction. And measure how much of the total variance each direction explains. Steps four and five are new today.

title.text:
Projecting onto the first principal component
turns 2 numbers per student into 1

objects.alt: Projecting onto the first principal component turns 2 numbers per student into 1

objects.text: The eight centred marks from Session 5. Each dot drops straight onto the red arrow, the first principal component.

runs.text: The red dots on the arrow are the projections.
A score is the position of the red dot along the arrow, in mark points.
The dashed lines show what is lost.

slides.notes:
These are the eight students from Session 5, centred. The red arrow is the first principal component, direction zero point eight, zero point six. Each dot drops straight onto the arrow along a dashed line, and the red dot is its projection. The position of the red dot along the arrow is a single number, the score of that student, measured in mark points.

The first student sits at minus seven, minus five, and has a score of minus eight point six. So two numbers per student have become one. The dashed lines are short, which tells us that very little is lost. In a round blob of dots they would be long.

title.text:
A score is a dot product with the principal
component, and explained variance is a ratio

objects.alt: A score is a dot product with the principal component, and explained variance is a ratio

rows.text: Principal component 1: the top eigenvector of C, length 1. Its entries are v₁₁ and v₁₂.
Centred marks of student i, as a column: maths mᵢ and physics pᵢ.
The score: the dot product v₁ᵀxᵢ.
Eigenvalues of C: the variances along each direction.
Share of the variance kept by component 1.

objects.text: Keep the first component and drop the second: 98.1 percent of the variance is kept, 1.9 percent is lost.

slides.notes:
Two formulas do the work. The score of a student is the dot product of the principal component v one with the student's centred marks, maths m i and physics p i. For the first student, minus seven and minus five, zero point eight times minus seven plus zero point six times minus five is minus eight point six.

The explained variance ratio is the eigenvalue of the component divided by the total of all eigenvalues. Here one hundred two over one hundred four, which is ninety-eight point one percent. So keeping one number per student keeps almost all the information about how the students differ, and one component is enough.

title.text:
Worked by hand: the eight scores,
and the variance they keep

objects.text: The scores have mean 0 and variance 102 (sum of squares 714, divided by n − 1 = 7). The squared distances dropped add up to 14, which is 7 × 2.

slides.notes:
All eight scores follow the same rule: zero point eight times the centred maths mark plus zero point six times the centred physics mark. The scores run from -15.0 to 13.0. Their mean is zero because the data were centred. Their variance, the sum of squares divided by seven, which is n minus one as in Session 5, is 102, the first eigenvalue.

That is the meaning of an eigenvalue of the covariance matrix. The squared distances from the dots to the arrow, the dashed lines, add up to 14, which is seven times the second eigenvalue. So the second eigenvalue measures what we throw away.

title.text: PCA is the SVD of the centred data

objects.alt: PCA is the SVD of the centred data

rows.text: The centred data, one row per student and one column per mark.
Its columns are the principal components, the same as the eigenvectors of C.
Variance along component i: σ² over n − 1, the sample variance of Session 5.
The columns of UΣ are the scores of all rows at once.

objects.text: Libraries use the SVD because it is more accurate than forming C first. Component signs may differ.

slides.notes:
This links today and last session. Take the centred data matrix X c and compute its SVD. The columns of V are the principal components, the same directions as the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix. The variance along component i is sigma i squared divided by n minus one.

For our marks the singular values are 26.72 and 3.74, and their squares divided by seven give one hundred two and two. Libraries compute PCA this way because it is more accurate than forming the covariance matrix first. Signs of components may differ between tools, and both are correct.

title.text: Four habits that keep SVD and PCA honest

rows.text: Running PCA on data that is not centred
The first direction then points at the mean, not at the spread.
A column in thousands dominates a column in units.
Divide each centred column by its standard deviation, the square root of its variance (z-scores, Session 14).
Treating a component as a named feature
It is a mix of all columns, and its sign is arbitrary.
Read the weights, and expect sign flips.
Keeping the most terms that fit
Small singular values often hold only noise.
Choose k with a rule, and check on held-out data.

slides.notes:
Four things to remember. First, centre the data before PCA. Without centring, the first direction points towards the mean instead of along the spread. Second, mind the scales. A column measured in thousands would dominate a column measured in units, so when the units differ, divide each centred column by its standard deviation, the square root of the variance from Session 5.

These are called z-scores, and Session 14 uses them again. Third, a component is a mix of all the columns, and its sign is arbitrary, so do not read it as a single named feature. Fourth, do not keep every term that fits. Small singular values often hold only noise.

title.text:
One function, np.linalg.svd, gives
the low-rank image and the PCA

runs.text: U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(M)
Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(Xc, full_matrices=
False
scores = Xc @ Vt[0]
ratio = S ** 2 / np.sum(S ** 2)

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: U, S, Vt = ... svd of any matrix M, such as the noisy image. S is a list, largest first.
M2 = ... scales the first 2 columns of U by their singular values, then multiplies by the first 2 rows of Vt.
Xc = ... centres X. full_matrices=False keeps only the columns of U that are needed (2 here, not 8).
scores = ... dots each row with component 1. ratio = ... is the explained variance.

slides.notes:
The code is six lines. np dot linalg dot svd returns three things: U, the singular values as a plain list from largest to smallest, and V transpose. M is any matrix, for example the noisy image. For a low-rank approximation, take the first two columns of U, scale each by its singular value, and multiply by the first two rows of V transpose.

For PCA, centre the data X, take its SVD, and the first row of V transpose is the first principal component. The setting full matrices equals False keeps only the two columns of U we need instead of eight. Multiply the centred data by the component to get the scores. The last line is the explained variance ratio.

Six lab steps, from a 2 by
2 SVD to the LoRA count

title.text:
Step 5 without an SVD function:
power iteration on NᵀN, then deflation

objects.text: N is the noisy image. M = NᵀN is symmetric, and its top eigenvalue is σ₁².
Power iteration
From all ones, ten rounds of multiply by M, divide by the largest entry: 1357.6 = σ₁², so σ₁ = 36.85.
Rank 1 term
v₁ = final guess at length 1, u₁ = Nv₁ / σ₁. σ₁u₁v₁ᵀ is a column times a row.
Deflation
M₂ = M − σ₁²v₁v₁ᵀ removes the top eigenvalue. Repeat: σ₂ = 15.07. Once more: σ₃ = 4.89.
Errors
Errors from the clean H: 15.40, 4.54, 6.73 for ranks 1, 2, 3, as the library gives.

slides.notes:
Neither Excel nor Google Sheets has an SVD function, so step five gets the singular values with Session 5. M equals N transpose N is symmetric, and its top eigenvalue is the first singular value squared. Run power iteration on M from a start of all ones, ten times.

The largest entry settles at 1357.6, so sigma one is 36.85. Scale the guess to length one to get v one, and u one is N times v one over sigma one. To get the next one, subtract sigma one squared times v one v one transpose from M, the same column-times-row pattern, and repeat.

That is called deflation. The errors match the library numbers, so both tracks reach the same answers.

slides.notes:
Four things will happen to someone. First, np dot linalg dot svd gives you the singular values as a plain list of numbers. Use np dot diag to turn it into a diagonal matrix, or scale the columns of U as in the recipe. title.text:
Where this appears in AI: LoRA trains two
thin matrices in place of one huge one

objects.alt: Where this appears in AI: LoRA trains two thin matrices in place of one huge one

objects.text: Illustrative sizes. LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) keeps W frozen (unchanged) and trains only B and A.

slides.notes:
This is the same mathematics in a published method. Training a model means adjusting its weights in small steps so that its errors shrink, and Sessions 7 to 10 show how. Fine-tuning means training an already trained, or pre-trained, model a little more on new data. Large language models of this kind have enormous weight matrices, so fine-tuning every number is expensive.

The LoRA paper, by Hu and colleagues in 2021, keeps the weight matrix W frozen and learns the change as a product of two thin matrices, B and A, whose shared inner size r is small. A thousand by a thousand matrix has one million numbers, while B and A together have sixteen thousand.

title.text: Where this appears in AI: LoRA in numbers

objects.alt: Where this appears in AI: LoRA in numbers

rows.text: The pre-trained weight matrix, d by d. Frozen: left unchanged.
Thin, d by r and r by d, trained. A new A, unrelated to today's A.
Numbers trained with LoRA against a full update.
B starts at zero, so the model begins as the original.

objects.text: B and A are learned by training (Sessions 7 to 10); no SVD is computed. Open models such as Llama allow this.

slides.notes:
LoRA in numbers: the updated weights are the frozen weights W plus the product B times A. If W is d by d, then B is d by r and A is r by d. This A is a new matrix, unrelated to the small matrix A from the start of today.

Only B and A are trained. With d equal to a thousand and r equal to eight, which are illustrative sizes, that is sixteen thousand trained numbers against one million for a full update, which is 1.6 percent. The paper starts B at zero, so the model begins as the original.

B and A are found by the training steps of the coming sessions, and the SVD only explains why a low-rank change can be enough. What closed products do internally is not public, so I will not claim it for them.

A short activity. Open any assistant you use and ask for the singular values of the matrix with rows two, two and minus one, two. You know the answer: three and two. Then ask how many numbers LoRA trains for a thousand by a thousand matrix with r equal to eight.

You know that too: sixteen thousand. Ask it to show its working and read it for slips. Assistants can make arithmetic errors, and checking against your own numbers is the skill. Never paste confidential data.

title.text:
Exit check: the three moves,
choosing k, and why LoRA is cheap

rows.text: What are the three moves of the SVD?
Rotate (Vᵀ), stretch (Σ, the singular values), rotate again (U).
How do you choose how many components to keep?
Use the cumulative explained variance, the elbow of the scree plot, or a test on the real task.
Why does LoRA train fewer numbers than a full update?
It trains two thin matrices B (d by r) and A (r by d) with small r, instead of one d by d matrix.

objects.text: Write your own answer first, then compare. Your lab checks are part of the exit check.
